arXiv:2607.26820v1 [cs.LG] 29 Jul 2026

Forecasting Trajectory-Level Safety Risks in Black-Box Multi-Turn Interactions

Shi Lin    Peng Qian\corresponding    Dinghao Liu    Renjie Sun    Sifan Wu    Dezhang Kong    Chenpei Wang    Xun Wang
Abstract

As large language models (LLMs) evolve from standalone assistants into autonomous agents, ensuring their safety requires shifting beyond pointwise risk assessment to understand how risks emerge and unfold over long-horizon trajectories. In multi-turn interactions, malicious intent can be decomposed across seemingly harmless turns and gradually reconstructed through interaction trajectories, eventually resulting in safety failures. Existing safeguards remain largely reactive, detecting manifested violations while lacking the ability to predict latent risk evolution and enable preemptive prevention. To address this limitation, we propose Recast, a safety risk forecasting framework that advances LLM safeguarding beyond turn-level violation detection to trajectory-level risk prediction. Recast first retrieves risk-relevant evidence from both short-term dialogue progression and long-term historical context via a dual-scale trajectory view. It then models compositional risk evolution by capturing the current risk configuration and its temporal dynamics. Finally, a causal temporal encoder learns latent risk evolution patterns and predicts the distribution of future risk emergence turns. Extensive experiments across 7 risk categories show that Recast predicts 88.3%88.3\% of future safety failures with an average lead time of 2.412.41 turns, while maintaining a false alarm rate of 12.3%12.3\%, showcasing the effectiveness of trajectory-level forecasting in identifying emerging risks before safety violations occur.

1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence is undergoing a revolutionary transition from passive language understanding to autonomous decision-making, largely driven by the emergence of large language models (LLMs) (Achiam et al. 2023; Anthropic 2023; Touvron et al. 2023; Grattafiori et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2025; Guo et al. 2025; Liu et al. 2024a; Glm et al. 2024). Beyond achieving remarkable capabilities in reasoning (Qin et al. 2023; Zhong et al. 2023), programming (Zhang et al. 2023), translation (Peng et al. 2023), and mathematics problem solving (Wei et al. 2022), LLMs are increasingly powering agentic systems capable of autonomously executing complex long-horizon tasks (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2024c). Unlike conventional dialogue systems that respond independently to individual prompts, LLM-based agents must continuously maintain memory, update task states, and make decisions based on evolving interaction histories. In this context, multi-turn interaction is no longer merely an extension of dialogue, but a fundamental process underlying agentic intelligence.

This paradigm transition also reshapes the safety landscape of agentic systems. Existing efforts have largely focused on single-turn scenarios, where the main goal is to determine whether a prompt can directly induce unsafe model behavior (Zou et al. 2023; Wei, Haghtalab, and Steinhardt 2023; Chao et al. 2025; Mehrotra et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2024b; Yu et al. 2024; Lin et al. 2024; Ding et al. 2024). However, in multi-turn interactions, harmful objectives can be strategically decomposed into a sequence of locally coherent and seemingly benign requests, each of which appears harmless in isolation but collectively drives the model towards malicious outcomes (Russinovich, Salem, and Eldan 2025; Yang et al. 2024; Li et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2025; Ren et al. 2025; Weng et al. 2025; Rahman et al. 2025; Kong et al. 2025). Therefore, safety risks in agentic systems cannot be viewed as solely pointwise prompt-level violations, but trajectory-level phenomena arising from the temporal accumulation and semantic composition of interactions.

Notwithstanding increasing efforts devoted to multi-turn interaction safety, existing approaches remain inherently retrospective (Inan et al. 2023; Ghosh et al. 2025; Han et al. 2024; Zeng et al. 2024a; Zhao et al. 2025; Shen et al. 2026; Ma et al. 2026). They usually analyze observed dialogue contexts and leverage historical turns as evidence for assessing the safety of the current response. While effective at identifying manifested violations, these methods provide limited understanding of how risks accumulate and transform throughout interaction trajectories, making it difficult to anticipate future safety failures before they occur. This limitation is particularly critical for multi-turn attacks, where individual turns may appear benign but progressively compose risk-relevant configurations that enable future misuse. This raises an important yet largely unexplored question: given an evolving interaction trajectory, can we forecast whether and when it will transition into an unsafe state in future turns?

Addressing this challenge requires shifting from retrospective detection to proactive trajectory-level forecasting. Multi-turn safety risk is neither a simple aggregation of per-turn risks, nor a static property of dialogue history. Instead, it emerges dynamically as new interactions reorganize previously observed evidence and alter its safety relevance. A seemingly benign turn may reinforce existing risk factors and gradually form configurations that precede future violations. Therefore, effective forecasting requires modeling compositional risk evolution and anticipating trajectories that may transition towards unsafe states. Motivated by this, we formulate multi-turn safety as a compositional risk evolution problem, aiming to characterize how evolving interaction trajectories give rise to future safety violations.

To this end, we propose Recast, a trajectory-level safety risk forecasting framework for black-box multi-turn interactions. Instead of estimating the risk of the current observed dialogue, Recast forecasts whether and when the interaction trajectory will evolve towards future safety failures. Recast consists of three key components: (i) Risk-relevant historical evidence retrieval. Recast captures complementary temporal dependencies by retrieving risk-relevant evidence from both short-term dialogue progression and long-term historical context. (ii) Compositional risk state and transition modeling. It constructs a structured risk state from retrieved evidence and models its temporal evolution via state transitions, capturing both risk composition and trajectory dynamics. (iii) Future risk distribution forecasting. A causal temporal encoder learns latent evolution patterns and predicts the distribution of future risk emergence over subsequent turns.

Extensive experiments on 7 risk categories demonstrate the effectiveness of Recast in modeling future risk trajectories, achieving a negative log-likelihood of 0.450.45 and a mean absolute error of 0.310.31 for first-risk emergence time forecasting. Furthermore, Recast predicts 88.3%88.3\% of future safety failures with an average lead time of 2.412.41 turns while maintaining a false alarm rate of 12.3%12.3\%, showing its capability to provide proactive warnings before explicit violations occur.

In summary, we make the following key contributions.

  • •

    We introduce a new perspective on the safety of multi-turn LLMs by shifting the objective from turn-level violation detection to trajectory-level safety risk forecasting, enabling early identification of emerging unsafe behaviors.

  • •

    We propose Recast, a safety risk forecasting framework that integrates historical evidence retrieval, structured risk state modeling, and causal trajectory inference to capture the evolution of latent risks during multi-turn interactions.

  • •

    Extensive experiments across 7 risk categories demonstrate that Recast accurately forecasts future risk trajectories and provides effective early warning, anticipating 88.3%88.3\% of safety violations with an average lead time of 2.412.41 turns while maintaining a 12.3%12.3\% false alarm rate.

2 Problem Formulation

We consider a black-box multi-turn interaction between a user and a target LLM. At turn ii, the user submits a request uiu_{i} and receives a response aia_{i}. The observed interaction trajectory up to turn tt is denoted as τ≤t=[(u1,a1),…,(ut,at)]\tau_{\leq t}=[(u_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,(u_{t},a_{t})]. After each turn, the safeguard only observes the textual trajectory τ≤t\tau_{\leq t}, without access to the model parameters, hidden states, logits, system prompts, or internal safety mechanisms. Unlike conventional safeguards that examine whether the current response violates safety policies, we study trajectory-level risk forecasting, aiming to predict whether and when the ongoing interaction will evolve into a future safety risk.

Formally, let t⋆t^{\star} denote the first turn at which the interaction trajectory exhibits a predefined safety risk. At any pre-risk turn t<t⋆t<t^{\star}, the remaining time to risk emergence is defined as dt=t⋆−td_{t}=t^{\star}-t. Given a forecasting horizon HH, our goal is to learn a predictor F⁡(⋅)F(\cdot) that estimates the conditional distribution of future risk emergence: F⁡(τ≤t)→𝝅tF(\tau_{\leq t})\rightarrow\bm{\pi}_{t}, where 𝝅t=[πt​(1),…,πt​(H),πt(>H)]\bm{\pi}_{t}=[\pi_{t}(1),\ldots,\pi_{t}(H),\pi_{t}(>H)] is a discrete time-to-risk distribution. For each h∈{1,…,H}h\in\{1,\ldots,H\}, πt​(h)=P⁡(dt=h∣τ≤t)\pi_{t}(h)=P(d_{t}=h\mid\tau_{\leq t}) represents the probability that the safety risk emerges exactly hh turns after the current turn, whereas πt(>H)=P⁡(dt>H∣τ≤t)\pi_{t}(>H)=P(d_{t}>H\mid\tau_{\leq t}) represents the probability that no safety risk emerges within the next HH turns. Therefore, 𝝅t\bm{\pi}_{t} characterizes both the likelihood of future risk emergence and its expected occurrence time.

3 Method

Method overview. Motivated by the observation that multi-turn safety risks emerge through evolving interaction trajectories, we propose Recast, a trajectory-level safety risk forecasting framework. Unlike existing safeguards that detect manifested risks in observed dialogues, Recast predicts how current interactions may evolve towards future safety violations. Our key insight is to model multi-turn safety as compositional risk evolution: seemingly benign dialogue fragments can be reactivated and recomposed by subsequent turns into risk-prone configurations. These configurations form the current risk state, while state transitions characterize their temporal evolution and provide signals for future risk forecasting. As illustrated in Figure 2, Recast consists of three components: (1) risk-relevant historical evidence retrieval, which extracts evidence from short-term progression and long-term context; (2) compositional risk state and transition modeling, which constructs risk states and captures their evolution across turns; and (3) future risk distribution forecasting, which employs a causal temporal encoder to predict the distribution of future risk emergence times.

Risk-Relevant Historical Evidence Retrieval

Given the current interaction turn, Recast retrieves risk-relevant evidence from both short-term progression and long-term historical context, capturing complementary temporal dependencies for trajectory-level safety risk forecasting.

Interaction turn representation. For each turn ii, we concatenate the user request uiu_{i} and model response aia_{i}, and encode the combined text into a shared semantic space using a pretrained text encoder Enc⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Enc}(\cdot):

𝒗i=Enc⁡(ui,ai)+pi,\bm{v}_{i}=\operatorname{Enc}\bigl(u_{i},a_{i}\bigr)+p_{i}, (1)

where pip_{i} is a learned positional embedding indicating the position of turn ii. This representation preserves both dialogue semantics and temporal structure across interaction turns.

Short-term progression. The short-term progression embraces recent trajectory dynamics, reflecting how emerging interactions gradually alter the direction of the dialogue. We augment each historical representation with adjacent-turn differences and apply windowed self-attention:

𝑳<t=LocalTrw⁡([𝒗i;𝒗i−𝒗i−1;𝒗i+1−𝒗i]i=1t−1),\bm{L}_{<t}=\operatorname{LocalTr}_{w}\left(\left[\bm{v}_{i};\bm{v}_{i}-\bm{v}_{i-1};\bm{v}_{i+1}-\bm{v}_{i}\right]_{i=1}^{t-1}\right), (2)

where LocalTrw\operatorname{LocalTr}_{w} restricts attention within a window of radius ww. The resulting 𝑳<t\bm{L}_{<t} therefore captures local interaction dynamics and short-term risk progression.

Long-term historical context. Local context alone may fail to capture distant factors that are reactivated as the dialogue evolves, such as latent objectives or prerequisite constraints. To model these long-term dependencies, we introduce KK learnable memory queries to retrieve complementary information from the dialogue trajectory:

𝑴<t=[𝒎1(t);…;𝒎K(t)]=MHAttn⁡(𝑸mem,𝑳<t,𝑳<t),\bm{M}_{<t}=[\bm{m}^{(t)}_{1};\ldots;\bm{m}^{(t)}_{K}]=\operatorname{MHAttn}(\bm{Q}_{\mathrm{mem}},\bm{L}_{<t},\bm{L}_{<t}), (3)

where MHAttn⁡(Q,K,V)\operatorname{MHAttn}(Q,K,V) denotes multi-head attention and 𝑸mem∈ℝK×d\bm{Q}_{\mathrm{mem}}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} contains learnable memory queries. The memory slots 𝑴<t\bm{M}_{<t} preserve diverse long-term dependencies in the dialogue trajectory, overcoming the limitations of local-window retrieval and coarse historical summarization.

Cross-path evidence retrieval. Not all historical information contributes equally to future risk forecasting. Its relevance depends on how it is connected to the current trajectory. A newly observed turn may either extend recent progression or reactivate earlier factors, requiring the model to consider both short-term dynamics and long-term dependencies. Therefore, we use 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t} as a query to retrieve evidence from these two paths, producing representations at complementary temporal scales. Short-term retrieval captures locally evolving risk patterns, while long-term retrieval identifies earlier factors that have been reactivated by subsequent interactions.

𝒆tloc\displaystyle\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{t} =f⁡(𝒗t+MHAttn⁡(𝒗t,𝑳<t,𝑳<t)),\displaystyle=f\!\left(\bm{v}_{t}+\operatorname{MHAttn}(\bm{v}_{t},\bm{L}_{<t},\bm{L}_{<t})\right), (4)
𝒆tmem\displaystyle\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}}_{t} =f⁡(𝒗t+MHAttn⁡(𝒗t,𝑴<t,𝑴<t)),\displaystyle=f\!\left(\bm{v}_{t}+\operatorname{MHAttn}(\bm{v}_{t},\bm{M}_{<t},\bm{M}_{<t})\right),

where 𝒆tloc\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{t} summarizes recent progression relevant to the current turn, and 𝒆tmem\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}}_{t} captures earlier information reactivated by the interaction at turn tt. We incorporate 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t} through a residual connection, allowing each evidence vector to retain both the current-turn semantics and retrieved historical context. The shared mapping function ff transforms the two evidence vectors into a common representation space. Using 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t} as the retrieval query, historical relevance becomes context-dependent, enabling the same historical information to contribute differently as the trajectory evolves.

Compositional Risk State and Transition Modeling

Future risk emergence depends not only on what evidence is retrieved, but also on how different evidence sources are composed and evolve along the interaction trajectory. Based on the retrieved evidence, Recast constructs a compositional risk state 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t} to characterize the risk-relevant information at turn tt and models a transition representation 𝒓t\bm{r}_{t} to capture its temporal evolution across turns, providing a structured representation of risk dynamics for future forecasting.

Compositional risk state construction. At turn tt, a risk state 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t} represents how recent progression and reactivated long-term history are integrated. Although the two evidence views provide complementary information, modeling them independently cannot capture their cross-temporal interactions. Such interactions are crucial because evidence fragments that appear benign individually may become predictive when jointly forming a coherent risk pattern. Therefore, we explicitly encode their feature-wise conjunction to construct the compositional risk state.

𝒔t=ϕstate​([𝒆tloc;𝒆tmem;𝒆tloc⊙𝒆tmem]),\bm{s}_{t}=\phi_{\mathrm{state}}\!\left([\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{t};\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}}_{t};\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{t}\odot\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}}_{t}]\right), (5)

where ϕstate​(·)\phi_{\mathrm{state}}\left(\textperiodcentered\right) is a feed-forward state encoder, and ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication that describes aligned feature activations between the two temporal views. By concatenating the two evidence views and their cross-temporal interaction, 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t} provides a structured representation of the current evidence composition, enabling the model to capture risk-relevant configurations before explicit violations occur.

Risk state transition modeling. The risk state 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t} captures the current composition of risk-relevant evidence but lacks temporal dynamics. To model how risk evolves across turns, we introduce the risk transition representation 𝒓t\bm{r}_{t}, which characterizes changes from turn t−1t-1 to turn tt. Specifically, 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t} describes the current risk configuration, while 𝒓t\bm{r}_{t} captures the temporal variation of its evidence components. For each 𝒙∈{𝒆loc,𝒆mem,𝒆tloc⊙𝒆tmem}\bm{x}\in\{\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}},\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}},\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{t}\odot\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}}_{t}\}, we compute the signed difference Δ​𝒙t=𝒙t−𝒙t−1\Delta\bm{x}_{t}=\bm{x}_{t}-\bm{x}_{t-1} and define the transition representation as:

𝒓t=ϕtrans​([Δ​𝒆tloc;Δ​𝒆tmem;Δ⁡(𝒆tloc⊙𝒆tmem)]),\bm{r}_{t}=\phi_{\mathrm{trans}}\!\left([\Delta\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{t};\Delta\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}}_{t};\Delta(\bm{e}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{t}\odot\bm{e}^{\mathrm{mem}}_{t})]\right), (6)

where ϕtrans​()\phi_{\mathrm{trans}}\left(\right) denotes a feed-forward transition encoder. Specifically, the three transition components reflect changes in recent progression, variations in reactivated long-term historical context, and changes in their cross-temporal composition, respectively. These transition components allow the model to distinguish different forms of trajectory evolution. Exactly, 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t} represents the current risk configuration, while 𝒓t\bm{r}_{t} models its temporal evolution, providing a trajectory-aware representation for future risk forecasting.

Future Risk Distribution Forecasting

Intuitively, forecasting future risk requires modeling not only the current turn state but also the trajectory through which it emerges. With the temporal risk states and transitions, Recast employs a causal temporal encoder to learn latent evolution patterns and predict the distribution of future risk emergence across multiple horizons.

Causal risk evolution encoding. We arrange the risk states and transitions at every turn into a temporal order [(𝒔1,𝒓1),…,(𝒔t,𝒓t)][(\bm{s}_{1},\bm{r}_{1}),\ldots,(\bm{s}_{t},\bm{r}_{t})]. This sequence characterizes both the risk configuration at each turn and the dynamics leading to the current state. We then apply a causal temporal encoder:

𝑮≤t=CausalTr⁡([(𝒔1,𝒓1),…,(𝒔t,𝒓t)]),\bm{G}_{\leq t}=\operatorname{CausalTr}([(\bm{s}_{1},\bm{r}_{1}),\ldots,(\bm{s}_{t},\bm{r}_{t})]), (7)

where the causal mask prevents access to unobserved future turns. Temporal self-attention interprets each state and transition within the context of the preceding trajectory. To this end, the encoded sequence retains both the current risk condition and the evolution through which it was reached, enabling the model to recognize recurring state-transition patterns and identify future risks.

Future risk distribution prediction. The final trajectory representation 𝒈t∈𝑮≤t\bm{g}_{t}\in\bm{G}_{\leq t} encodes the causal evolution patterns observed up to turn tt. We feed 𝒈t\bm{g}_{t} into a forecasting head to predict the time-to-risk distribution:

𝝅t=softmax⁡(𝑾π​𝒈t+𝒃π),\bm{\pi}_{t}=\operatorname{softmax}(\bm{W}_{\pi}\bm{g}_{t}+\bm{b}_{\pi}), (8)

where 𝝅t\bm{\pi}_{t} represents the predicted distribution of future risk emergence over the forecasting horizon. It enables Recast to estimate both the likelihood and timing of future risks without explicitly modeling future dialogue trajectories.

Training objectives. For each observed turn t<t⋆t<t^{\star}, where t⋆t^{\star} denotes the ground-truth risk turn, we define the time-to-risk label as yt=min⁡(t⋆−t,H+1)y_{t}=\min(t^{\star}-t,H+1), where H+1H+1 denotes risks occurring beyond the forecasting horizon. We optimize the predicted distribution with the negative log-likelihood.

ℒFF=−∑tlogπt(yt),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FF}}=-\sum_{t}\log\pi_{t}(y_{t}), (9)

The overall training objective incorporates three auxiliary objectives: ℒord\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ord}} enforces monotonic risk escalation towards failure, ℒrank\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}} promotes consistent risk ordering among samples, and ℒben\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ben}} reduces false alarms on benign interactions.

ℒ=ℒFF+λord​ℒord+λrank​ℒrank+λben​ℒben.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FF}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{ord}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ord}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rank}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{ben}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ben}}. (10)

This enables end-to-end optimization of the proposed framework, allowing all components to be trained without requiring explicit supervision of intermediate representations.

4 Experiment

We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of Recast, seeking to answer the following questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Can Recast accurately forecast safety risks and reduce the success rate of multi-turn jailbreak attacks? How about the additional latency introduced by Recast?

  • •

    RQ2: How effective is Recast under diverse forecasting settings and interaction conditions?

  • •

    RQ3: How does each component of Recast contribute to trajectory-level safety risk forecasting?

  • •

    RQ4: Does Recast capture interpretable risk evolution patterns before explicit safety violations emerge?

Experimental Setup

Training dataset. To model multi-turn risk evolution, we construct a safety trajectory dataset through a four-stage pipeline. First, we collect multi-turn attack trajectories from public resources and normalize them to balance risk categories and attack patterns. Second, we perform controlled length augmentation and align trajectory-length distributions to mitigate length bias. Third, we generate hard benign samples by transforming risk-inducing turns into safety-oriented contexts, enabling the model to distinguish genuine risk evolution from benign analysis of sensitive topics. Finally, we unify all samples into a standardized format and split the dataset to avoid evaluation leakage. The resulting dataset contains 10,000 trajectories, including 5,000 harmful and 5,000 benign samples across 7 risk categories.

Testing dataset. For comprehensive evaluation, we adopt AdvBench (Zou et al. 2023) and SORRY-Bench (Xie et al. 2025), comprising 960 harmful behaviors in total.

Metrics. We evaluate Recast from three main perspectives. (i) Risk forecasting. Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) measures the probability assigned to the ground-truth risk emergence turn, while Expected-MAE measures the deviation between predicted and actual risk times. (ii) Early warning. After each turn, we compute the risk score Rt=1−P⁡(dt>H)R_{t}=1-P(d_{t}>H) and trigger warnings when Rt>τaR_{t}>\tau_{a}. Early warning rate (EWR), False alarm rate (FAR), and Mean lead turn (MLT) measure warning coverage, false alarms, and lead time, respectively. (iii) Online defense. We evaluate practical effectiveness by measuring Δ​ASR\Delta\mathrm{ASR}, i.e., the reduction in attack success rate compared with the undefended setting.

Attack baselines. We evaluate Recast against 4 multi-turn attack methods: ActorAttack (Ren et al. 2025) and Red Queen (Jiang et al. 2025), which are included in training and constitute seen attack families; and ICON (Lin et al. 2026) and X-Teaming (Rahman et al. 2025), which are strictly excluded from training and serve as unseen attack families for evaluating cross-attack generalization.

Safeguard baselines. We compare 5 safeguard baselines from 3 categories: Guardrail model, including Llama-Guard-3-8B (Inan et al. 2023) and Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B (Zhao et al. 2025); History-aware safeguards, including THRD (Ma et al. 2026); and Prompt-based defenses, including Intent Analysis (Zhang et al. 2025) and LLM-as-Judge (Perez et al. 2022).

Target models. We evaluate all attacks on 3 representative LLMs, including GPT-4o-2024-11-20, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen2-7B-Instruct. To ensure deterministic results, we set both temperature and top_p to 00.

Hyperparameters and device. We use the frozen bge-large-en-v1.5 encoder to obtain 1024-dimensional representations for each user-assistant turn. We train Recast for 24 epochs using AdamW with a batch size of 64, learning rate of 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}, and weight decay of 10−210^{-2}. We repeat all experiments with three random seeds {42,43,44}\{42,43,44\} and report the average performance. All experiments are conducted on an Ubuntu 20.04 platform with an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8255C CPU and eight NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs.

RQ1: Forecasting and Defense Capability

Early warning defense. We first investigate whether the forecasting capability of Recast can enhance defense against multi-turn attacks. After each dialogue turn, Recast monitors the interaction trajectory and triggers an early warning when the predicted risk exceeds the threshold τa\tau_{a}. As shown in Table 1, Recast reduces the average ASR from 71.5%71.5\% to 45.9%45.9\%, achieving comparable defense performance to the strongest history-aware safeguard baseline, THRD (45.7%45.7\%). Furthermore, combining Recast with Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B further reduces the ASR to 40.4%40.4\%. These results demonstrate that trajectory-level risk forecasting captures complementary risk signals to conventional safeguards. Recast enables proactive risk interception, while guardrail models provide additional protection against residual unsafe outputs.

Risk forecasting. Next, we evaluate if Recast can accurately forecast future safety risks before explicit violations emerge. As shown in Table 2, Recast achieves an NLL of 0.450.45 and an Expected-MAE of 0.310.31, showing its ability to accurately estimate the distribution of future risk emergence. By converting the predicted distribution into a future risk score, Recast achieves an EWR of 88.3%88.3\% with an average MLT of 2.412.41 turns, while maintaining a FAR of 12.3%12.3\%. These results suggest that Recast can identify emerging safety risks before they materialize into explicit violations, instead of merely detecting unsafe behaviors after occurrence.

Category-wise forecasting. We also examine the generalization capability of Recast across seven risk categories. As shown in Table 2, Recast achieves effective early warning across diverse safety domains, while exhibiting category-specific variations. It obtains the highest EWR on Privacy Violation (94.3%94.3\%), Sexual & Child Exploitation (91.7%91.7\%), and Physical Harm (88.6%88.6\%), whereas Chem & Bio Harm presents the lowest EWR (77.1%77.1\%). Regarding false alarms, Misinformation & Hate achieves the lowest FAR (2.4%2.4\%), while Privacy Violation shows a relatively higher FAR (24.6%24.6\%). Cybersecurity remains the most challenging category for temporal forecasting, achieving an NLL of 0.560.56 and an Expected-MAE of 0.410.41. These results indicate that Recast learns transferable trajectory-level risk patterns across diverse harm domains, while highlighting the need for category-aware calibration in practical deployments.

Latency Overhead. Finally, we measure the additional latency introduced by Recast during trajectory-level risk forecasting. As shown in Table 3, Recast incurs an average overhead of 48.148.1ms per turn across three LLMs, accounting for only 1.4%1.4\% of the corresponding LLM response latency. The results indicate that Recast achieves effective risk forecasting with negligible impact on interaction efficiency.

RQ2: Robustness Evaluation

Forecasting horizon robustness. We investigate the impact of forecasting horizon HH on the risk prediction capability of Recast. As shown in Figure 3, increasing HH from 11 to 55 leads to higher forecasting uncertainty, with NLL increasing from 0.180.18 to 0.640.64 and Expected-MAE from 0.170.17 to 0.430.43. This trend is expected, as predicting more distant risk emergence requires reasoning over increasingly uncertain future trajectories. Meanwhile, extending HH from 11 to 33 improves early warning performance, increasing EWR from 83.3%83.3\% to 88.3%88.3\% and reducing FAR from 18.2%18.2\% to 12.3%12.3\%. Long-range forecasting is subject to greater uncertainty, which limits the gains that can be made when looking at a wider horizon. Overall, H=3H=3 achieves a favorable trade-off between forecasting accuracy, warning coverage, and prediction distance.

Dialogue length sensitivity. We next evaluate Recast under dialogues of different lengths, including short (≤3\leq 3 turns), medium (4−74-7 turns), and long (≥8\geq 8 turns) trajectories. As shown in Figure 4, longer interactions provide richer contextual evidence and improve risk forecasting accuracy. Specifically, NLL decreases from 0.630.63 on short dialogues to 0.290.29 on long dialogues, while Expected-MAE decreases from 0.470.47 to 0.210.21. The EWR also increases from 79.4%79.4\% to 93.2%93.2\%, accompanied by an increase in FAR from 5.3%5.3\% to 19.3%19.3\%. These results indicate that longer trajectories enable more accurate risk evolution modeling and broader warning coverage, while introducing additional opportunities for false alarms due to increased contextual complexity.

Warning threshold sensitivity. We finally analyze the sensitivity of Recast to the warning threshold τa\tau_{a}. As shown in Figure 5, increasing τa\tau_{a} from 0.30.3 to 0.70.7 reduces FAR from 18.6%18.6\% to 9.8%9.8\%, while EWR decreases moderately from 91.8%91.8\% to 85.7%85.7\%. Meanwhile, MLT decreases from 3.323.32 to 2.072.07 turns, reflecting a more conservative warning strategy with shorter intervention windows. These results demonstrate that Recast provides flexible threshold calibration: lower thresholds favor higher warning coverage and earlier intervention, whereas higher thresholds reduce unnecessary interruptions in benign interactions.

RQ3: Ablation Study

To evaluate the contribution of individual components in Recast,we perform an ablation study by removing each module independently. The results are reported in Table 4.

Short-term progression modeling. Removing the short-term progression modeling while retaining long-term context increases Expected-MAE by 16.1%16.1\% and FAR by 57.7%57.7\%. This show that recent trajectory dynamics provide essential signals for anticipating imminent risk emergence and prevent excessive dependence on distant historical context.

Long-term context retrieval. Removing long-term context retrieval increases NLL by 15.6%15.6\% and decreases EWR by 8.5%8.5\%. This suggests that local dialogue progression alone cannot capture the risk factors that were introduced earlier and reactivated during subsequent interactions.

Cross-path evidence composition. Removing the explicit interaction between short-term and long-term evidence results in the largest degradation in Expected-MAE and FAR, increasing them by 22.6%22.6\% and 58.5%58.5\%, respectively. This highlights the importance of modeling cross-temporal evidence composition for identifying emerging risk patterns.

Risk state transition modeling. Removing risk state transitions causes the largest drop in NLL (17.8%17.8\%) and EWR (9.2%9.2\%). This verifies that modeling temporal state evolution provides predictive signals beyond static risk configurations.

RQ4: Interpretable Risk Evolution Analysis

Risk evolution before safety violations. We first analyze whether Recast captures distinguishable risk evolution patterns before explicit safety violations emerge. For each harmful-benign pair, we compare their predicted risks at the same distance dd before the risk emergence point. As shown in Figure 6, the average risk gap between harmful and benign trajectories increases from 0.150.15 to 0.410.41, 0.560.56, and 0.690.69 as the unsafe outcome approaches. Meanwhile, the average risk score of harmful trajectories increases from 0.210.21 to 0.830.83, whereas benign trajectories remain consistently low (0.060.06 to 0.140.14). These results indicate that Recast can identify emerging risk signals before explicit violations and progressively separate unsafe trajectories from benign ones.

Representative case. We then investigate a representative case involving vehicle theft. As shown in Figure 7, both harmful and benign trajectories initially discuss vehicle theft prevention techniques over the first 4 turns, and Recast assigns low risk scores to both trajectories (≤0.11\leq 0.11). At turn 5, the harmful trajectory begins to compose previously discussed information into a vulnerability-oriented context, causing the risk score to increase sharply to 0.850.85 and exceed the warning threshold τa=0.5\tau_{a}=0.5, while the prevention-oriented trajectory remains at a low risk level. At turn 6, the harmful trajectory transforms scattered vulnerability information into an actionable theft procedure, leading to an explicit safety violation. Recast successfully issues a warning two turns before the violation while avoiding false alarms on the benign trajectory. Additional case studies are provided in the appendix.

5 Related Work

Safety risks in multi-turn interactions. Recent studies reveal that safety risks in LLMs can emerge from the cumulative evolution of multi-turn interactions. Crescendo (Russinovich, Salem, and Eldan 2025) gradually escalates benign conversations toward harmful objectives; Red Queen (Jiang et al. 2025) hides malicious intent in harm-prevention contexts; ActorAttack (Ren et al. 2025) exploits semantically related interactions; and FITD (Weng et al. 2025) decomposes unsafe goals into progressive requests. More adaptive attacks, such as X-Teaming (Rahman et al. 2025) and Tempest (Zhou and Arel 2025), further leverage agent collaboration or search-based optimization to refine attack trajectories. However, existing studies focus on improving attack effectiveness and provide limited insight into how safety risks evolve throughout interactions. In contrast, Recast investigates risk evolution at the trajectory level and forecasts emerging safety risks before explicit violations occur.

Defenses against multi-turn attacks. Existing safeguards for multi-turn risks can be categorized into three groups. Guardrail models, including Llama Guard (Inan et al. 2023), Qwen3Guard (Zhao et al. 2025), WildGuard (Han et al. 2024), and ShieldGemma (Zeng et al. 2024a), classify the safety of observed inputs or outputs. Prompt-based defenses leverage LLM reasoning to assess intent and safety, including Intent Analysis (Zhang et al. 2025), LLM-as-Judge (Perez et al. 2022), and AutoDefense (Zeng et al. 2024b). History-aware safeguards, such as THRD (Ma et al. 2026) and TurnGate (Shen et al. 2026), incorporate dialogue history to improve risk assessment. Nevertheless, these approaches are largely retrospective, detecting risks manifested in observed interactions rather than forecasting future risk evolution. Unlike previous safeguards, Recast formulates multi-turn safety as a trajectory-level forecasting problem, predicting the likelihood of future safety risks before violations emerge.

6 Conclusion

We study trajectory-level safety risk forecasting for black-box multi-turn interactions, shifting the focus of multi-turn safeguards from retrospective detection to proactive risk anticipation. We propose Recast, which retrieves risk-relevant evidence from short-term dialogue progression and long-term historical context. It then constructs structured risk states and models their temporal evolution to forecast the distribution of future risk emergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Recast accurately predicts risk evolution and provides effective early warnings before explicit safety violations occur. Our work highlights the potential of trajectory-level modeling for building proactive multi-turn safeguards.

Appendix A Appendix

Details of Evaluation Metrics

We provide detailed definitions of the evaluation metrics used in our experiments. For a dialogue trajectory τ\tau, let τ≤t\tau_{\leq t} denote the dialogue observed up to turn tt, referred to as the current dialogue state. Let Tf∈ℕ∪∞T_{f}\in\mathbb{N}\cup{\infty} be the first turn at which a safety failure occurs. Here, Tf=∞T_{f}=\infty indicates that no safety failure occurs in the trajectory. The remaining time-to-failure at turn tt is defined as

dt={Tf−t,Tf<∞,∞,Tf=∞.d_{t}=\begin{cases}T_{f}-t,&T_{f}<\infty,\\ \infty,&T_{f}=\infty.\end{cases}

Given a forecasting horizon HH, the ground-truth first-failure bucket is defined as follows:

yt={dt,1≤dt≤H,H+1,otherwise,y_{t}=\begin{cases}d_{t},&1\leq d_{t}\leq H,\\ H+1,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

where the bucket H+1H+1 corresponds to the case where the first failure occurs beyond the forecasting horizon HH or no failure occurs. Recast predicts a categorical distribution 𝝅t=[πt​(1),…,πt​(H),πt​(H+1)],\bm{\pi}_{t}=\left[\pi_{t}(1),\ldots,\pi_{t}(H),\pi_{t}(H+1)\right], where πt​(h)\pi_{t}(h) denotes the predicted probability that the first failure will occur after hh turns, and πt​(H+1)\pi_{t}(H+1) denotes the probability of no failure within the forecasting horizon.

To evaluate the quality of warnings, we convert the predicted first-failure distribution into a future risk score:

Rt=1−πt​(H+1)=∑h=1Hπt​(h).R_{t}=1-\pi_{t}(H+1)=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\pi_{t}(h).

This score represents the probability that the current dialogue will lead to a safety failure within the next HH turns.

Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL). The NLL measures whether the model assigns a high probability to the ground truth first failure bucket.

NLL=−1|𝒮|∑t∈𝒮logπt(yt),\mathrm{NLL}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{S}}\log\pi_{t}(y_{t}),

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} denotes the set of all evaluated dialogue states. A lower NLL indicates better distributional forecasting quality.

Expected-MAE. We convert the predicted distribution into an expected failure time:

d^t=∑h=1H+1h⋅πt​(h).\hat{d}_{t}=\sum_{h=1}^{H+1}h\cdot\pi_{t}(h).

The ground-truth distance is clipped into the finite bucket range d~t=yt\tilde{d}_{t}=y_{t}. Expected-MAE is then computed as

Expected​-​MAE=1|𝒮|​∑t∈𝒮|d^t−d~t|.\mathrm{Expected\text{-}MAE}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{S}}\left|\hat{d}_{t}-\tilde{d}_{t}\right|.

A lower value indicates a more accurate estimation of the number of turns remaining before failure.

Early Warning Rate (EWR). Given a warning threshold, τa\tau_{a}, the first warning time of a trajectory is defined as follows:

ta​c​c=min⁡{t∈𝒯⁡(τ)∣Rt≥τa},t_{acc}=\min\left\{t\in\mathcal{T}(\tau)\mid R_{t}\geq\tau_{a}\right\},

where 𝒯⁡(τ)\mathcal{T}(\tau) denotes the set of turns at which Recast is evaluated for trajectory τ\tau. If no dialogue state exceeds the threshold, ta​c​c​(τ)t_{acc}(\tau) is undefined and the trajectory is treated as not having been warned.

Let 𝒟h​a​r​m\mathcal{D}_{harm} denote the set of harmful trajectories with a valid first failure turn. EWR measures the proportion of harmful trajectories that are warned before the first failure:

EWR=|{τ∈𝒟h​a​r​m∣ta​c​c​(τ)<Tf​(τ)}||𝒟h​a​r​m|.\mathrm{EWR}=\frac{\left|\left\{\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{harm}\mid t_{acc}(\tau)<T_{f}(\tau)\right\}\right|}{\left|\mathcal{D}_{harm}\right|}.

False Alarm Rate (FAR). Let 𝒟b​e​n\mathcal{D}_{ben} denote the set of benign trajectories. FAR measures the proportion of benign trajectories that trigger a warning:

FAR=|{τ∈𝒟b​e​n∣ta​c​c​(τ)​ is defined}||𝒟b​e​n|.\mathrm{FAR}=\frac{\left|\left\{\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{ben}\mid t_{acc}(\tau)\text{ is defined}\right\}\right|}{\left|\mathcal{D}_{ben}\right|}.

Mean Lead Turn (MLT). MLT measures how many turns earlier the model raises a warning before the first failure, averaged over successfully warned harmful trajectories:

MLT=1|𝒟w​a​r​n|​∑τ∈𝒟w​a​r​n(Tf​(τ)−ta​c​c​(τ)).\mathrm{MLT}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{warn}|}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{warn}}\left(T_{f}(\tau)-t_{acc}(\tau)\right).

where

𝒟w​a​r​n={τ∈𝒟h​a​r​m∣ta​c​c​(τ)<Tf​(τ)}.\mathcal{D}_{warn}=\left\{\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{harm}\mid t_{acc}(\tau)<T_{f}(\tau)\right\}.

Attack Success Rate (ASR). For deployment evaluation, the ASR measures the proportion of multi-turn jailbreak attempts that eventually succeed:

ASR=# of successful attack trajectories# of all attack trajectories ×100%.\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{\text{\# $\textit{of successful attack trajectories}$}}{\text{\# $\textit{of all attack trajectories}$ }}\times 100\%.

Once the risk score exceeds τa\tau_{a}, we terminate the interaction. An attack is considered successfully intercepted only when the warning is triggered before the annotated failure turn.

ASR Reduction (Δ​ASR\Delta\mathrm{ASR}). Finally, Δ​ASR\Delta\mathrm{ASR} measures the relative reduction in attack success rate compared with the no-defense setting:

Δ​ASR=ASRno​-​defense−ASRdefenseASRno​-​defense×100%.\Delta\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{no\text{-}defense}}-\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{defense}}}{\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{no\text{-}defense}}}\times 100\%.

Construction of Training Dataset

In multi-turn interactions, harmful objectives are often not explicitly revealed in a single request but gradually emerge through the accumulation and composition of seemingly benign turns. Therefore, our data construction aims to capture how distributed risk signals evolve into safety failures, enabling trajectory-level risk forecasting. The construction follows three principles:

  • •

    Broad attack coverage. The dataset should encompass diverse risk categories and attack strategies, allowing the model to learn generalizable risk evolution patterns rather than specific attack templates.

  • •

    Temporal progression signals. The dataset should preserve how risks develop across turns, with each harmful trajectory annotated by its first-failure turn to provide supervision for forecasting.

  • •

    Challenging benign counterparts. The dataset should include hard benign trajectories that share similar topics, terminology, and progression patterns with harmful ones but remain safe, encouraging the model to distinguish risk evolution from superficial similarities.

Based on these principles, we construct the training corpus through a four-stage pipeline.

Stage 1: Diverse Source Curation and Regularization. We collect multi-turn attack trajectories from three public sources: CKA-Agent, Red Queen, and ActorAttack. Despite their different attack mechanisms, these methods decompose harmful objectives into sequences of plausible subgoals. To improve diversity and reduce distribution bias, we map all samples to a unified risk taxonomy and perform balanced sampling across risk categories and attack strategies.

Stage 2: Trajectory Length Expansion. Short trajectories provide limited evidence of risk evolution, while length imbalance may introduce spurious correlations between dialogue length and safety labels. We thus expand trajectories to increase their average length and balance the length distribution. Harmful trajectories are extended by adding contextual setup and intermediate subgoals while preserving their original intent. Corresponding benign trajectories are expanded with comparable length and progression patterns but without leading to safety failures, reducing length-based bias.

Stage 3: Hard Benign Trajectory Construction. To prevent the model from relying on sensitive topics or keywords, hard benign trajectories are constructed that preserve the context of harmful counterparts while transforming failure-supporting structures into defence-oriented reasoning. Specifically, an auxiliary LLM first identifies turns that support failure, another LLM then rewrites these towards safe objectives and a safety evaluator finally verifies that the resulting trajectory remains harmless. While the resulting pairs share similar surface characteristics, they differ in their organisation of information: harmful trajectories accumulate evidence towards unsafe outcomes, whereas benign trajectories redirect the same context towards safe resolutions.

Stage 4: Unified Annotation and Standardization. Finally, we consolidate all constructed samples into a unified corpus and convert them into a standardized format. This includes trajectory content, risk category, attack strategy, and failure annotations. To verify annotation reliability, we additionally conduct human verification on a random subset of 1,000 responses, obtaining an agreement rate over 86% with the original annotations. All identified disagreements are subsequently adjudicated and corrected.

Additional Experimental Results

Cross-attack generalization. We also investigate whether Recast transfers beyond the attack structures observed during training. Tables 5 and 6 separately report the results on seen attack families (ActorAttack and Red Queen) and unseen families (ICON and X-Teaming). Specifically, Recast reduces the average ASR to 55.3%55.3\% on unseen attacks, corresponding to a 31.6%31.6\% relative reduction, while reducing it to 36.6%36.6\% on seen attacks with a 41.2%41.2\% reduction. When combined with Qwen3Guard, the ASR is further reduced to 48.5%48.5\% and 32.3%32.3\% on unseen and seen attacks, yielding relative reductions of 39.9%39.9\% and 48.2%48.2\%, respectively. These results demonstrate that the learned trajectory-level risk signals transfer to attack families that are absent from training, while the remaining seen-unseen gap reflects the additional challenge introduced by cross-attack distribution shifts.

Structured risk modeling gains. We further examine whether Recast provides more accurate and reliable risk warnings than direct sequence forecasters trained under the same setting. We compare it with GRU, Transformer, and a 5.41M parameter-matched Transformer to control for model capacity. As shown in Table 7 and Figure 8, Recast reduces NLL by 4.1−11.9%4.1-11.9\% and Expected-MAE by 7.3−22.3%7.3-22.3\%, demonstrating consistently more accurate estimation of future risk emergence. The most pronounced practical advantage lies in false alarm control, where Recast reduces FAR by 31.3−46.1%31.3-46.1\%. Importantly, this substantial reduction is not achieved by suppressing warnings, since Recast simultaneously improves EWR by 1.0−2.6%1.0-2.6\%, showing its superior warning reliability. Its consistent advantage over the parameter-matched Transformer further shows that the improvement comes from the proposed forecasting design rather than additional model capacity.

Additional Analysis of Case Study

We analyze a case from the Financial Crime category concerning vehicle anti-theft mechanisms. The harmful trajectory seeks actionable assistance for bypassing these defence mechanisms, whereas the benign counterpart discusses the same technical factors for auditing and prevention. Table 8 summarizes the key semantics of the dialogue.

How Prior Context Supports Warning. Figure 9(a) examines the effect of context on warnings. Removing the broad trend context in T1 reduces the risk score of T5 to 0.7240.724, whereas removing T2, T3, or T4 lowers it to 0.1250.125, 0.0040.004, and 0.2280.228, respectively. The particularly decrease after removing T3 indicates that linking target vehicles to theft methods is critical when T5 reframes the discussion around defensive gaps. Therefore, the warning depends not on T5 alone, but on how it connects evidence from earlier turns.

How Forecast Evolves Toward Failure. Figure 9(b) shows how the forecast evolves towards failure. After T4 lists multiple anti-theft technologies, the harmful branch still assigns 0.8980.898 probability to d>3d>3, indicating that sensitive technical content alone does not trigger a warning. After T5 links these defences through their integration gaps, this probability falls to 0.1500.150, while the mass shifts to d=2d=2 (0.4130.413) and d=3d=3 (0.4200.420), yielding a within-horizon risk of 0.8500.850. At T6, when the user asks how to defeat the disconnected layers systematically, the risk rises to 0.9990.999, one turn before the annotated T7 failure. In contrast, the benign branch also discusses the same topic but refuses exploit-oriented requests and keeps T5 focused on prevention, retaining 0.9950.995 probability on d>3d>3. The forecast therefore captures how information develops across turns rather than focusing on the topic alone.

Figure 9(c) shows that this change is not due to the passage of time. Compared with the T4 distribution shifted forward by one bucket, the harmful forecast after T5 changes substantially (JSD =0.362=0.362), whereas the benign forecast remains almost unchanged (JSD <0.001<0.001). Thus, the shift towards near-term failure is driven by the new relationship introduced at T5 and not by a simple reduction in remaining distance.
